title: Characterisation of lung function trajectories and associated early-life predictors in an Australian birth cohort study.
ehr_evidence: Our study included participants from the Raine Study, a prospective pregnancy cohort, with at least two spirometry measurements. Clinical and demographic data were collected during pregnancy and offspring assessed before birth and at 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 10, 14, 17, 18, 20, 22, 27 and 28 years of age.
summary: In a prospective Australian birth cohort (Raine Study) of 1512 participants with two or more spirometry measurements, group-based trajectory modelling identified FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC trajectories from 6 to 22 years and multinomial logistic regression linked early-life predictors (asthma, maternal smoking, PM2.5Absorbance) to low lung function trajectories.
key_findings: Four distinct lung function trajectories were identified for FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC (z-scores) from 6 to 22 years.

Childhood asthma at age 6 was associated with the low FEV1 trajectory (RRR 1.68, 95% CI 1.20–2.36) and with the very low (RRR 3.31, 95% CI 2.01–5.47) and low–average (RRR 1.98, 95% CI 1.21–3.24) FEV1/FVC trajectories.
Maternal smoking both in pregnancy and at age 6 was associated with the very low FEV1/FVC trajectory (RRR 2.47, 95% CI 1.52–2.50); smoking only in pregnancy or only at age 6 showed no association.
Early-life PM2.5Absorbance was associated with the low FEV1 trajectory (RRR 1.63, 95% CI 1.06–2.51) and inversely with the average–low FEV1/FVC trajectory (RRR 0.52, 95% CI 0.35–0.79).
NO2 exposure showed no significant association with any trajectory (e.g. FEV1/FVC average–low RRR 0.90, 95% CI 0.84–0.96).
Low birthweight/preterm birth was associated with the low–average FEV1/FVC trajectory (RRR 1.77, 95% CI 1.02–3.08; preterm RRR 2.03, 95% CI 1.11–3.71).
Males were more likely to belong to the very low FVC trajectory; socioeconomic status, respiratory infections, paternal eczema and parental hay fever were not associated with trajectories.
Atopy aeroallergens only or combined was associated with lower risk of the average–low FEV1/FVC trajectory (RRR 0.70, 95% CI 0.51–0.95).
captured_features: FEV1 z-score spirometry at 6, 14 and 22 years
FVC z-score spirometry at 6, 14 and 22 years
Parental asthma, eczema, hay fever, smoking and education
study_design: Prospective birth cohort (longitudinal) with group-based trajectory modelling
data_source_type: birth cohort (Raine Study, research-collected spirometry and questionnaire data)
population: 1512 Raine Study participants (768 males, 744 females) from Perth, Western Australia, assessed from childhood (6 years) to young adulthood (22 years)
exposure_domain: Air pollution (PM2.5Absorbance, NO2), maternal/smoking exposure, childhood asthma, plus familial and socioeconomic early-life factors
limitations: High dropout rate and over-representation of children with more respiratory symptoms attending follow-up visits.
Respiratory symptoms recorded by parental recall, not molecular/clinical confirmation.
Spirometry may be suboptimal at age 6, potentially underestimating FVC and inflating FEV1/FVC.
Air pollution exposure was back-extrapolated over 19 years and measured only from age 3–4, missing in utero and early postnatal lung development.
Low air pollutant concentrations in Perth limit generalisability.
Pregnancy complications and chronic parental/child diseases were excluded due to small numbers.
